👨‍👩‍👧 For grown-ups — curriculum & how Hoot teaches · tap to open
📍 Curriculum state: Connecticut

Ages 2–13 are mapped to Connecticut's own frameworks — CT Early Learning & Development Standards for little ones, then Connecticut Core Standards, NGSS science and CT Social Studies Frameworks. Pick another state and the paths re-map when that state's edition is added.

🌿 Montessori, woven through Hoot's World

Connecticut sets what children learn; Montessori sets how — by hand, by choice, at the child's own pace. Every Learning Path carries a green Montessori box with the hands-on work behind it, and the Work Shelf further down is a real shelf your child can work through right here. No timers, no scores.

🌿 The five Montessori ideas behind Hoot's World — tap to read
Follow the childThe child chooses the work and repeats it as long as they need. Hoot suggests — he never drags.
Hands before symbolsSizes, quantities and letters are touched and moved first. Names and numerals come after the hand already knows.
Control of errorThe material itself shows a mistake — a bead in the wrong jar just looks wrong — so children correct themselves, no red X needed.
Prepared environmentOne work per tray, everything complete and in its place, on a low shelf a child can reach. Order outside builds order inside.
Real work, real purposePouring, carrying, sorting and caring for living things are curriculum, not a break from it — especially under age 7.

🌞 Monday's adventures

🌳

Leaf Hunt Walk

Take a little basket or bag outside and hunt together for 3 different leaves — one big, one small, one that has changed colour. Carry them home carefully in two hands, then line them up on the table.

🌳 OutdoorAbout 15 min
🧱

Tallest Tower

Blocks, cushions or empty boxes: build the tallest tower you can. Count the pieces out loud as it grows — then knock it down together and build it again, even taller.

🏠 IndoorAbout 15 min

🌞 Tuesday's adventures

💧

Puddle Play

After rain, find a puddle — or make one with a watering can. Float a leaf boat, splash in boots, and test what floats and what sinks: a stone, a leaf, a stick.

🌳 OutdoorAbout 15 min
🥄

Spoon Carry Race

Two bowls and a spoon each. Carry pom-poms, cotton balls or pasta shapes from one bowl to the other, one at a time — slow, careful hands win this race.

🏠 IndoorAbout 15 min

🌞 Wednesday's adventures

🐞

Bug & Bird Watch

Sit very still outside for one whole minute — garden, park or balcony. Who spots a bird, a bee or a beetle first? Count together how many you see.

🌳 OutdoorAbout 10 min
🎨

Finger-Paint the Weather

Paint today's weather with fingers: a big yellow sun, grey swirly clouds or blue rain streaks. Name every colour as you go, then hang it up to dry.

🏠 IndoorAbout 15 min

🌞 Thursday's adventures

🪨

Stone Sort

Collect 5 stones on a short walk. Line them up biggest to smallest, then wash them in a bowl of water together and watch their colours change.

🌳 OutdoorAbout 20 min
🛋️

Cushion Obstacle Path

Cushions to climb over, a blanket tunnel to crawl through, a tape line to walk along. Go round and round — then rearrange it together and go again.

🏠 IndoorAbout 15 min

📸

Photo Quest Walk

Today's outdoor mission: find one thing that changed this week — a new flower, a taller plant, a chalk drawing — and photograph it together. Its photo spot is right here on this card.

🌳 OutdoorAbout 20 min
🧦

Sock-Puppet Story

Two clean socks become two puppets. They say hello, sing a song and tell one tiny story — then swap puppets, and the kids make the voices.

🏠 IndoorAbout 10 min

🏖️

Dig & Discover

Sandpit, beach or a big tray of sand or soil: dig, pour, fill and tip. Hide 3 treasures — shells, big buttons, toy animals — then dig to find them all again.

🌳 OutdoorAbout 20 min
🍌

Little Chefs Snack

Wash hands first, then make a real snack together: banana slices to count and share, or crackers and cheese to stack. Carry it to the table carefully, two hands.

Cloud Watching

A blanket on the grass or in the park: lie back and watch the clouds drift past. What do they look like — a sheep, a boat, a dragon? Count 5 clouds together.

Build a blanket fort over two chairs, climb inside with a torch and a favourite picture book, and take turns "reading" the pictures to each other.

🪵 The Work Shelf

Choose a work — carry it carefully, work as long as you like, put it back ready for the next child.

9 WORKS · 4 MADE FOR AGES 2–4

Just like a real Montessori shelf: the child picks one work, carries it carefully, works as long as they like, and puts it back ready for the next child. All nine works below really work — and four of them are made just for ages 2–4, with the biggest targets and the fewest steps. Slowly is exactly right.

Colour Bead Sorting Sensorial · Ages 2–7

Pick up one bead at a time, look at its colour, then tap the jar it belongs to. If a bead lands wrong, its colour tells you itself — that's control of error. One at a time, no rushing.

The tray is ready. Tap a bead to pick it up.

At home: a muffin tin, three colours of big buttons or dry beans, and one tray. Set it on a low shelf and let your child discover it — finished means every bead home and the tray back on the shelf.

The Pink Tower Sensorial · Ages 2–7

Montessori's most famous material: cubes one size-step apart, teaching size to the eye and hand long before numbers name it. Tap the cubes biggest to smallest and watch your tower build itself, one careful cube at a time.

Which cube is the biggest? Begin there.

At home: stack five food boxes or wooden blocks biggest to smallest, then carry them back one by one. Knocking it down and starting again isn't failure — repetition is how the learning happens.

Pouring Practice Practical Life · Ages 2–7

Real Montessori practical life: pour slowly, watch the water climb, and stop right at the red line — not over it. Spilled? In a Montessori classroom you wipe it up calmly yourself, and pour again. Concentration is the lesson.

🫗
stop line

The glass is empty. Pour a little at a time.

At home: a small jug half-full of water, one glass, a tray underneath and a sponge beside it for spills. Five quiet minutes before breakfast is a complete Montessori work.

Spoon Transfer — Pom-Poms Practical Life · Ages 2–4

Made for the very littlest hands: pick up ONE soft pom-pom, carry it slowly on the spoon, and tip it into the empty bowl. One at a time — if it drops, you just pick it up and try again. Steady hands and watching eyes are the whole lesson.

The tray is ready. Tap a pom-pom to pick it up with the spoon.

At home: cotton balls or craft pom-poms, one spoon and two bowls on a tray. Start with the biggest, fluffiest pom-poms — they are the easiest to balance — and let your child repeat it as many times as they like.

Water the Flowers Care of Plants · Ages 2–4

Five little sprouts are thirsty. Tap a sprout to give it a drink and watch it bloom! Caring for living things — gently, one at a time — is real Montessori work, and the very first science: plants need water to grow.

Five dry little sprouts, waiting. Tap a sprout to water it.

At home: one real plant and a tiny watering can or cup your child can carry with two hands. One plant that is truly theirs to water — and check on every morning — teaches care better than any lecture.

Shape Sorter Sensorial · Ages 2–4

Made for little hands, just like Spoon Transfer: pick up ONE shape, look at its edges, then tap the hole that is the same shape. A shape only fits its own hole — if it doesn't go in, turn it over in your mind and look again. That's control of error, no grown-up marking needed.

The tray is ready. Tap a shape to pick it up.

At home: a real shape sorter, or a cardboard box with a circle, square and triangle cut into the lid and three matching blocks or lids to post through. Empty it together and start again — posting it in is only half the work; carrying it back to the shelf is the rest.

Hang the Washing Practical Life · Ages 2–4

Washing day! Pick up ONE wet thing from the basket, carry it to the line, and tap a peg to hang it up to dry. One at a time, peg by peg — real laundry work, sized for the smallest helpers in the house.

Five wet things in the basket. Tap one to pick it up.

At home: a low line or a drying rack your child can reach, a few of their own small things — socks, flannels, a T-shirt — and two pegs each. Squeezing a peg open is serious finger-strength work, and it is quietly building the hand that will one day hold a pencil.

Sound Cylinders Sensorial · Ages 3–7

Montessori's listening work: six cylinders that all look the same, but inside they sound different — two by two, they match. Tap a cylinder to shake it and listen, then find the one that sounds exactly the same. Your ears do all the work here; your eyes can't help you.

Tap a cylinder to shake it and hear its sound.

At home: six identical tubs with lids, in pairs — two with rice, two with dry pasta, two with coins. Tape the lids shut, mix them up, and match by shaking and listening only. Start with two pairs for little ears and add the third pair when they're ready.

Thread the Pattern Sensorial & Patterns · Ages 3–7

A necklace is started for you, and it follows a pattern. Look at the beads already on the string — say their colours out loud — then tap the bead colour that comes next to thread it on. Patterns are the very beginning of maths: noticing what repeats, and what must come after.

Thread on:

Look at the pattern on the string. What colour comes next?

At home: big beads or pasta tubes and a shoelace with a knot in one end. Start a red–blue–red–blue pattern and let your child finish the string; when that feels easy, try red–red–blue. Threading is slow, two-handed work — that slowness is the concentration building.

🌱 Learning Paths

Pick an age below. Hoot teaches each lesson first — with pictures and worked examples — then your child tries it and earns the star.

48 LESSONS · 16 FOR AGES 2–4

AGES 2–4Little Explorers Learning Path

Sixteen tiny lessons, in order. Hoot teaches each one with big pictures first — then your child taps the answer and earns the star. A few minutes at a time; no test, just stars.

Connecticut standards: CT Early Learning & Development Standards (CT ELDS) — the play-based framework Connecticut wrote for this age: language & literacy, mathematics, cognition, and social-emotional growth, learned through play, talk and doing — never worksheets or testing.

📖 How this path works: Hoot teaches, then you try. Everything in Hoot's lesson is tappable — colours splash, shapes trace themselves, letters wiggle and sound out, counting lights up one by one. Tap ▶ Show me again and Hoot re-teaches it live. Then tap the answer and earn the star.

⭐ 0 of 16 lessons done

1

Colour names

⭐

Colours have names. Look at each one and say its name out loud together:

REDYELLOWBLUE

The first one is RED — like a strawberry 🍓. Say it: “red!”

Your turn! Tap the RED one.

2

Shape names

⭐

Shapes have names too. A circle is round like a ball. A square has 4 straight sides. A triangle has 3 pointy corners — count them: 1, 2, 3!

Circle Square Triangle

Your turn! Tap the TRIANGLE — the one with 3 pointy corners.

3

Counting to 5

⭐

Counting means touching each thing one time and saying its number. Tap every apple and count out loud with Hoot:

One tap, one number — that's counting!

Your turn! ⭐⭐⭐ — how many stars are there?

4

First letter sounds

⭐

Letters make sounds. Say each sound out loud together:

A 🍎A says “ah” — Apple B 🎈B says “buh” — Balloon C 🐱C says “kuh” — Cat

Your turn! Which letter says “buh”?

5

Big and small

⭐

Some things are BIG and some are small. Look — say it out loud together:

🐘BIG elephant 🐭small mouse

The elephant takes up lots of room. The mouse takes up just a tiny bit!

Your turn! Tap the BIG one.

6

Counting back from 5

⭐

Counting can go backwards too — like a rocket getting ready to launch! Say it out loud together, slower and quieter… then BLAST OFF:

5 … 4 … 3 … 2 … 1 … 🚀

Each number is one LESS than the one before it.

Your turn! When we count back from 5, what number comes next?

7

More letter sounds

⭐

Three more letters, three more sounds. Say them out loud together:

D 🐶D says “duh” — Dog F 🐸F says “fff” — Frog G 🍇G says “guh” — Grapes

Your turn! Which letter says “duh”?

8

Sorting: things that go together

⭐

Sorting means putting things that are the same together. Look: all the RED things go in one pile, all the BLUE things in another:

🔴 Red pile
🍎 🚗 🎈 🔵 Blue pile
🧢 🐳 🫐

Everything in a pile matches that pile's colour!

Your turn! Here comes a RED strawberry 🍓. Which pile does it go in?

9

Counting to 10

⭐

After 5, the numbers keep going: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10! Tap every star and count all the way up with Hoot:

One tap, one number — all the way to 10!

Your turn! 🐥🐥🐥🐥🐥🐥🐥🐥 — how many ducklings are there?

10

More colours: green, orange, purple

⭐

Three more colours to name. Say each one out loud together:

GREENORANGEPURPLE

GREEN is grass 🌱, ORANGE is an orange 🍊, and PURPLE is grapes 🍇!

Your turn! Tap the GREEN one — the grass colour.

11

Animal sounds

⭐

Every animal has its own sound. Make them together — as loud as you like!

🐮Cow says “moo!” 🦆Duck says “quack!” 🐶Dog says “woof!”

Your turn! Who says “moo”?

12

Feelings faces

⭐

Faces show feelings. Look at each face and make it on your own face too!

😀HAPPY — big smile 😢Sad — wobbly mouth 😴Sleepy — closing eyes

Feelings are okay to have — and okay to say out loud: “I feel happy!”

Your turn! Tap the HAPPY face — the one with the big smile.

13

Up and down

⭐

Some things are UP high, and some are DOWN low. Point up, then point down as you say them:

⬆️ 🐦UP — bird in the sky ⬇️ 🐜DOWN — ant on the ground

Your turn! Tap the one that is UP.

14

Patterns: what comes next?

⭐

A pattern repeats the same thing, over and over. Look and say it out loud:

🔴 🔵 🔴 🔵 🔴 🔵

Red, blue, red, blue… after blue always comes red again! The pattern tells you what is next.

Your turn! 🍎 🍌 🍎 🍌 🍎 … what comes next?

⭐

⭐

🌿 The Montessori way — Practical Life & the Senses

For ages 2–4 Montessori begins with real, useful work sized for small hands, and with the senses. The big games are already full of it — here is the work behind the screen:

  • Practical Life: Pouring Practice on the Work Shelf is the classic first work — and the shelf now holds four works made just for ages 2–4: Spoon Transfer with soft pom-poms, Water the Flowers, the Shape Sorter, and Hang the Washing. At home it's a small jug, two cups and a tray — carrying, pouring and wiping spills build the concentration everything else stands on.
  • Sensorial: Colour Splash works like Montessori colour tablets, and Animal Friends' sounds work like sound cylinders — matching by eye and ear, with eyes closed for a challenge.
  • Control of error: Animal Homes corrects itself — the right home feels finished, the wrong one doesn't fit. No grown-up marking, no red X.
  • Same CT goal, Montessori route: the CT ELDS language, maths and social-emotional goals in this path are still the target — they're simply reached by hand first, on a tray, at the child's own pace.

AGES 5–7Early Readers Learning Path

Eight lessons, in order. Hoot teaches each idea first — a letter sound, a blending trick, counting on, rhyming, taking away, tens and ones — then your child tries it right here and earns the star. Sounds become words, words become stories, and counting becomes adding.

Connecticut standards: Connecticut Core Standards for English Language Arts & Mathematics — reading foundations and phonics in Kindergarten–Grade 2, counting and place value, and adding & subtracting within 20 by the end of Grade 2, plus CT's science expectations through observing the real world.

📖 How this path works: Hoot teaches, then you try. Hoot explains each idea in small steps — tap Next step ▶ to walk through the worked example together, and tap everything in the teaching picture: number lines light up, words flip, pieces shade in. Every lesson ends with a So remember line, and ▶ Show me again, Hoot! replays the whole teaching. Then answer the question and earn the star.

⭐ 0 of 8 lessons done

1

Letter sounds

⭐

Every letter makes its own sound. Say them out loud:

S 🐍“sss” — like a snake M 🐮“mmm” — like yummy food T 🐢“tuh” — a tiny tap sound

Reading starts here: know the sound, and you can start sounding out whole words.

Your turn! Which letter makes the “sss” snake sound?

2

Blend sounds into words

⭐

Blending means pushing letter sounds together until they become one word. Watch:

c … a … t  →  caaat  →  CAT 🐱

Say the sounds slowly, then faster and faster — the word pops out! This is how ALL reading works.

Your turn! Push these together: m … a … p. What word do you get?

3

Counting on to add

⭐

Adding trick: don't start from 1 — start from the big number and count on. Watch 3 + 2:

+

Hold “3” in your head… then count on for the red dots: 4, 5! So 3 + 2 = 5.

Your turn! 4 + 2 = ? Hold 4 in your head, then count on two more.

4

Read a line — and understand it

⭐

Reading isn't just saying words — it's picturing what they mean. Read this line out loud, word by word:

The cat sat on the mat.

Now picture it: a cat, sitting, on a mat. If you can see the picture in your head, you truly read it!

Your turn! In that line, WHO sat on the mat?

5

Rhyming words

⭐

Words rhyme when they end with the same sound. Listen: cat and hat both end in “at” — they rhyme! So do sun and run, with their “un” ending. Rhyming words are word cousins — and hearing rhymes makes reading easier.

Your turn! Which word rhymes with DOG?

6

Taking away

⭐

Adding puts more in. Taking away leaves less. Start with 5 apples and take 2 away to eat:

🍎🍎🍎🍎🍎

Count what's left: 1, 2, 3. So 5 − 2 = 3. The faded apples are the ones that got eaten!

Your turn! 6 − 2 = ? Start at 6, take 2 away, count what's left.

7

Tens and ones

⭐

Big numbers are built from tens and ones. Look at 14: it is ONE bundle of ten, plus 4 loose ones:

🧺 101 ten+🍎🍎🍎🍎4 ones

The first digit tells the tens, the last digit tells the ones. That's the secret code inside every number!

Your turn! In the number 23, how many TENS are there?

8

Answer questions about a story

⭐

Good readers can answer questions about what they read — the answers hide INSIDE the words. Read this line out loud:

The frog jumped into the pond.

Picture it: a frog, a big jump, a splash! Now hunt for the answer in the line.

Your turn! WHERE did the frog jump?

  • Reads a short story line aloud on their own
  • Counts to 20 and says what comes next
  • Adds two numbers up to 10 without fingers to start

🌿 The Montessori way — Sandpaper Letters & Golden Beads

This is the age Montessori children famously read and count early — because letters and quantities start in the fingers, not on a worksheet:

  • Sandpaper letters, screen-style: Balloon ABC Pop and Letter Sound Pop follow the Montessori order — hear the sound, see and trace the shape, then use it. Pip's Build-a-Word is the movable alphabet: sounds become words one letter at a time.
  • Golden Beads thinking: Count the Apples keeps quantity touchable before numerals stand alone, and Rocket Count-Up's counting-on grows out of handling real amounts first. At home, count stairs, spoons and socks into piles of ten.
  • Practical Life grows up: buttoning, pouring their own drink, setting the table and caring for a plant are this age's real homework — Leaf Detective is a Montessori nature walk: slow down, look closely, name what you find.
  • Freedom within limits: three missions a day, but the child chooses the order and may repeat a favourite. Repetition until it feels easy is the method working, not time wasted.

Connecticut standards: Connecticut Core Standards (ELA & Math — multiplication, fractions and reading to learn), the Next Generation Science Standards adopted by Connecticut (hands-on investigations, not memorising), and the Connecticut Social Studies Frameworks for inquiry and evidence.

⭐ 0 of 8 lessons done

1

Times tables are groups

⭐

3 × 4 means 3 groups of 4. Look at the dots — 3 rows of 4:

Count them in 4s: 4, 8, 12. So 3 × 4 = 12. Any times table is just groups you can count — you never have to guess.

Your challenge! 5 × 3 = ? (5 groups of 3 — count in 3s: 3, 6, 9…)

2

Fractions: equal parts

⭐

A fraction is a whole cut into equal parts. This pizza is cut in half — each piece is 1/2. Cut it into 4 and each piece is 1/4:


1/2 — one of 2 parts
1/4 — one of 4 parts

The trick everyone trips on: more parts means each part is SMALLER. So 1/2 is bigger than 1/4 — even though 4 is bigger than 2!

Your challenge! Which is the bigger slice?

3

Find the main idea

⭐

Strong readers ask: what is this whole text about? That's the main idea. Read this:

“Deep under a volcano, rock melts into magma. Pressure builds and builds — until the magma bursts out as lava, ash and gas. That explosion is an eruption.”

“Lava is hot” is true, but it's just one detail. The whole text explains one thing: how a volcano erupts.

Your challenge! What is the main idea of that text?

4

Coding: order matters

⭐

Code is a list of instructions a computer follows exactly, in order. This code — ➡ ➡ ⬆ — moves Hoot right, right, up. Swap the order and Hoot ends up somewhere completely different. Programmers plan the whole path before pressing run — try it for real in Code Hoot's Path above.

Your challenge! Hoot needs to go UP first, then RIGHT. Which code does that?

5

Division is sharing equally

⭐

Dividing is sharing equally — the opposite of multiplying. Share 12 cookies fairly between 3 friends: deal them out one at a time — round 1, round 2, round 3, round 4 — and each friend ends with 4. So 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Check it with your times tables: 3 × 4 = 12 ✓. Division and multiplication are a team.

Your challenge! 20 stickers shared equally among 4 friends. How many does each friend get?

6

How plants make food

⭐

Plants are food factories that run on sunshine. It's called photosynthesis: the roots drink water, the leaves catch sunlight and breathe in air — and the plant turns them into its own food, releasing the oxygen we breathe out the other side. Nearly every meal you have ever eaten started inside a leaf!

Your challenge! What do leaves mainly catch, to make the plant's food?

7

Topic sentences

⭐

A paragraph has ONE main idea, and its first sentence — the topic sentence — announces it. Read: “Bees are tiny flying farmers. One bee visits about 50 flowers on a single trip, carrying pollen from flower to flower as it goes…” Everything after the first sentence works to prove it. A weak opener like “Bees are insects” announces nothing worth proving.

Your challenge! Which is the strongest topic sentence for a paragraph about how dogs help people?

8

Area: length × width

⭐

Area measures how much flat space something covers — counted in squares. This rug is 4 squares long and 3 squares wide:

🟦🟦🟦🟦
🟦🟦🟦🟦
🟦🟦🟦🟦

Count them: 12 squares. The fast way is length × width: 4 × 3 = 12. Rows times columns, every time.

Your challenge! A garden is 5 squares long and 2 squares wide. What is its area?

🌿 The Montessori way — Great Stories, Materials & Going Out

Montessori calls ages 6–12 the age of the reasoning mind and the big question: how does everything connect? The Kingdom path answers the Montessori way:

  • Great Lessons: big, true stories — how volcanoes are born, how life began — spark the imagination first; the facts and Gatekeeper challenges follow the wonder, never the other way round.
  • Materials before memorising: maths in this path follows the Stamp Game and bead-chain idea — work the quantity with something real, then let symbols take over once the hand understands.
  • Classification walks: Real-World Adventures quests are Montessori botany and zoology in the wild: collect, sort, compare, name — then report back to the group, which is real science communication.

AGES 11–13Creators Learning Path

Eight maker lessons behind every project above. Each teaches a real skill with a worked example — ratios, trustworthy research, debugging, presenting, percentages, the design loop, evidence and budgets — then hands you a decision to make. Learn the skill here; use it in the projects.

Connecticut standards: Connecticut Core Standards for middle school — ratios and expressions in maths, research and argument writing in ELA — with NGSS middle-school science & engineering design and the CT Social Studies Frameworks, all practised inside real, finished projects.

📖 How this path works: learn the skill, then make the call. Hoot teaches each skill step by step — tap Next step ▶ to work the example one move at a time, with the reasoning (and plain-meaning glosses for the hard words) said out loud. Tap the teaching visuals to test claims, flip verdicts and run the numbers yourself. Each lesson ends with a So remember recap, and ▶ Show me again, Hoot! replays the teaching — then a real maker decision is yours.

⭐ 0 of 8 lessons done

1

Ratios: scale both sides

⭐

Your lemonade recipe is a ratio: 2 cups lemon : 3 cups water. Making a double batch? Double both sides — 4 : 6 — and it tastes identical. Scale only one side and the ratio breaks. Every recipe, map, model and mix in your projects works this way.

Your call! You're scaling up to 12 cups of water. How much lemon keeps the taste the same?

2

Research you can trust

⭐

Before any fact goes into your project, run the 3 checks: 1) Who wrote it — an expert or organisation you can name? 2) Can another source confirm it? 3) Is it informing you — or selling to you? A source that passes all three earns its place; one that fails gets dropped, however cool it sounds.

Your call! Which source is strongest for the Volcano Lab?

3

Debug: change ONE thing

⭐

The maker's rule when something breaks: change ONE thing, retest, write down what happened. Change three things at once and the build might work — but you'll never know which change fixed it, so you'll be stuck again next time. This is exactly what the Project Sprint above trains.

Your call! In your game, the jump is broken AND the sprite is the wrong colour. What's the first move?

4

Present: hook, build, land

⭐

Every strong presentation has the same skeleton: HOOK — one line that makes people care. BUILD — show the work, including what went wrong and what you changed. LAND — finish with what you'd do next. Beginning, middle, end — on purpose, not by accident.

Your call! Which opening is a real HOOK for the Volcano Lab?

5

Percentages: parts of 100

⭐

A percent is a slice of 100. The maker's shortcut: find 10% first — just move the decimal one place left — then build up. 10% of 240 playtesters is 24, so 25% is 24 + 24 + 12 = 60. Fundraising goals, discounts, battery bars and test scores all speak percent; now you can speak it back.

Your call! 50% of your 80 playtesters finished the demo. How many players is that?

6

The design loop: test, fix, retest

⭐

No first version survives contact with a real user — and that's the plan, not a failure. Professionals work in a loop: sketch it rough → test it on a real person → fix the ONE biggest problem → test again. Polish comes last, never first: a beautiful level nobody can finish is still a broken level.

Your call! Your first playtester gets stuck at the level-1 door for two whole minutes. What's the first move?

7

Make a claim — bring evidence

⭐

Persuasive writing is a claim carrying its proof. Weak: “Our film is the best.” — nothing there can be checked. Strong: “Our film holds attention because every scene ends on an unanswered question — test viewers named the cliffhangers as the reason they kept watching.” Claim, reason, evidence — in one breath.

Your call! Which sentence is a claim WITH evidence, for the Backyard Scientist journal?

8

Budget the project

⭐

Real projects run on real budgets, and a budget is just careful adding done before you spend. Volcano Lab budget: $60. Already spent: board $25 and paint $20 — that's $45, leaving $15. Every new cost gets checked against what's LEFT, not against the original $60. That one habit is the difference between finished projects and abandoned ones.

Your call! The eruption kit costs $12. Can the Volcano Lab afford it?

🎓 Kaitlyn's New York Tutor Lessons — Hoot teaches, step by step. Made for grade 7 in Port Chester, NY. Every lesson goes the same gentle way: 🔥 Warm-up (Lessons 2–8 start with one quick question from an earlier lesson) → 👀 Watch me (Hoot does one, thinking out loud) → 🤝 Try with me (we do one together) → ⭐ Your turn → 🎓 Teach it back (pick the sentence that explains the idea best — that's when the star lands). Tiny steps. No timers. No penalties — a wrong answer just means Hoot names the exact mix-up and explains it a different way.

New York standards: NY Next Generation Learning Standards for Maths & ELA, NYSSLS for science, and the NY Social Studies Framework — grade 7.

⭐ 0 of 8 NY lessons done

1

Unit rates: the price of ONE

⭐
NY Next Generation · Maths 7.RP — Ratios & Proportional Relationships
🦉

Hoo hoo, Kaitlyn! Today I'm your tutor for unit rates. Stores in Port Chester use these every day — they tell you what ONE of something costs, so you can spot the best deal. We'll go tiny-step by tiny-step.

📖 Words to know: a unit rate means the cost (or amount) for exactly 1 — like $7 for 1 ticket. Divide means share a total into equal parts.

👀 Watch me — I'll do one first

Step 1. Here's my problem: 6 concert tickets cost $42. I want the price of ONE ticket.

Step 2. To find the price of one, I share the total equally. I divide: 42 ÷ 6. Think: 6 × ? = 42.

Step 3. 6 × 7 = 42 — so 42 ÷ 6 = 7.

Step 4. So the unit rate is $7 per ticket. That word “per” is my clue — it always means “for 1”.

✅ That's the whole trick: total ÷ how many = price of one. Nice watching — noticing the steps is real learning.

🦉 Quick check, Kaitlyn

How is that sitting? No wrong answer here — I just want to know how to help.

A different way — picture it: Imagine 6 friends splitting a $42 pizza bill fairly. Nobody pays $42 — each person pays their one fair share. $42 shared by 6 people is $7 each. A unit rate is just a fair share — the price of one share.

🤝 Try with me — we do this one together

New problem, same trick: 4 notebooks cost $10. You tap each step — I'm right here.

Step 1: To find the price of ONE notebook, what do we divide?

✔️ Exactly — total ÷ how many. You picked the right setup. That's the hardest part, and you did it.

Step 2: What is 10 ÷ 4?

✔️ Unit rate: $2.50 per notebook. We did that one together — the next one is yours, and I know you can.

🎉 Together: done! Now show me your solo flight…

⭐ Your turn, Kaitlyn

8 juice boxes cost $24. What is the unit rate — the price of ONE juice box?

🦉 So remember: unit rate = total ÷ how many. “Per” means “for 1” — and dividing finds it every time.

2

Negative numbers on the number line

⭐
NY Next Generation · Maths 7.NS — The Number System
🦉

Hi Kaitlyn! Today: adding and subtracting negative numbers. Your school tests love these — and they get easy once you can see them on a number line. Watch my feet hop along the line.

📖 Words to know: a negative number is less than zero — like −3, three steps LEFT of zero. The number line is a path: adding walks right, subtracting walks left.

−6·−5·−4·−3start−2·−1·0·1·2·3·4land!5·6·7·8·
👀 Watch me — I'll do one first

Step 1. My problem: −3 + 7. I stand on −3 on the number line (find it above — it's lit up).

Step 2. I'm adding 7, so I walk RIGHT 7 hops: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

Step 3. I landed on 4. So −3 + 7 = 4.

Step 4. Notice: I passed zero on the way. Starting negative doesn't mean ending negative — a big enough walk right crosses zero!

✅ The line does the thinking: start at the first number, walk, land.

🦉 Quick check, Kaitlyn

How is that sitting? No wrong answer here — I just want to know how to help.

A different way — think temperature: It's −3° outside in Port Chester, and the day warms up by 7 degrees. −3, then warmer: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The thermometer ends at 4°. Same walk, same answer: −3 + 7 = 4.

🤝 Try with me — we do this one together

This one has a famous trap, and we'll disarm it together: 5 − (−2).

Step 1: Subtracting a negative flips it into adding. So 5 − (−2) becomes…?

✔️ You got the sign rule right that time — minus a negative becomes plus. That rule is the whole lesson!

Step 2: So what is 5 + 2?

✔️ 5 − (−2) = 7. Together: done. The trap didn't stand a chance.

🎉 Now one on your own — use the number line above any time. It's not cheating; it's the strategy!

⭐ Your turn, Kaitlyn

Use the number line: what is −4 + 9?

🦉 So remember: on the number line, adding walks right, subtracting walks left — and minus a negative flips to plus.

3

Two-step equations: unwrap x

⭐
NY Next Generation · Maths 7.EE — Expressions & Equations
🦉

Tutor time, Kaitlyn! Two-step equations look scary, but they're just presents: x is wrapped in two layers, and we unwrap them backwards. I'll unwrap one slowly, then we unwrap one together.

📖 Words to know: an equation is a balance — both sides weigh the same. Undo means do the opposite: the opposite of +5 is −5, and the opposite of ×3 is ÷3. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other — the balance stays fair.

👀 Watch me — I'll do one first

Step 1. My equation: 3x + 5 = 20. x was multiplied by 3, then 5 was added. I unwrap in REVERSE: last layer on, first layer off.

Step 2. Undo the +5 first: subtract 5 from BOTH sides. 3x + 5 − 5 = 20 − 5, so 3x = 15.

Step 3. Now undo the ×3: divide both sides by 3. 15 ÷ 3 = 5, so x = 5.

Step 4. Always check! 3 × 5 + 5 = 15 + 5 = 20 ✔️. The balance balances — I'm sure.

✅ Unwrap backwards: undo the adding first, then undo the multiplying — and check at the end.

🦉 Quick check, Kaitlyn

How is that sitting? No wrong answer here — I just want to know how to help.

A different way — think of a gift: x is a surprise inside a box (+5 of wrapping paper), inside a bag (×3 of ribbon). To open it you remove the LAST thing put on, first. Undo +5, then undo ×3. Same unwrapping — that's all an equation is.

🤝 Try with me — we do this one together

Our equation: 4x − 3 = 13. You lead, I steady the balance.

Step 1: x was multiplied by 4, then 3 was SUBTRACTED. Unwrapping backwards, what's the first move?

✔️ 4x = 16. You unwrapped in the right order — that's the skill!

Step 2: Now undo the ×4. What is x?

✔️ Check it: 4 × 4 − 3 = 13 ✔️. We solved it together. Solo flight next!

🎉 You've got the unwrapping order down. Your turn!

⭐ Your turn, Kaitlyn

Solve it your way: 2x − 4 = 10. What is x?

🦉 So remember: unwrap x backwards — undo the +/− first, then the ×/÷, keep both sides balanced, and always check.

4

Main idea & citing evidence

⭐
NY Next Generation · ELA 7R1 — Read closely & cite text evidence
🦉

Reading time, Kaitlyn — and this is the skill your teachers ask for most: find the main idea, then prove it with a sentence from the text. Detectives do exactly this. Let's be detectives.

📖 Words to know: the main idea is what the WHOLE text is mostly about, in one line. Evidence is a sentence from the text that proves your idea. To cite means to point at that exact sentence.

👀 Watch me — I'll do one first
“For many years, factories dumped waste into the Hudson River, and fish nearly disappeared. Then people got to work: towns cleaned the water, scientists tested it, and volunteers planted grasses along the banks. Today, striped bass and even eagles have returned to the river.”

Step 1. I ask: what does EVERY sentence talk about? The Hudson River — first dirty, then cleaned, then alive again.

Step 2. So the main idea covers the whole trip: “People helped the Hudson River recover.” Not just “fish” (one detail) — the whole change.

Step 3. Now I cite evidence — the sentence that proves people helped: “towns cleaned the water, scientists tested it, and volunteers planted grasses along the banks.”

Step 4. See the pattern? Main idea = the whole story in one line. Evidence = the sentence that proves it.

✅ Detective rule: never just say the idea — point at the sentence.

🦉 Quick check, Kaitlyn

How is that sitting? No wrong answer here — I just want to know how to help.

A different way — the umbrella: The main idea is an umbrella. Every sentence in the text should fit UNDER it. “Fish” is too small an umbrella — the cleaning sentences poke out. “People helped the river recover” covers everything. If a sentence pokes out, your umbrella (main idea) is too small.

🤝 Try with me — we do this one together
“Maya practised piano a little every day. At first her fingers stumbled over the keys. After two months of short daily practice, she played her first full song without stopping.”

Step 1: Which umbrella covers the WHOLE passage?

✔️ Right-sized umbrella! It covers the beginning, middle and end.

Step 2: Which sentence from the passage is EVIDENCE that practice worked?

✔️ You cited real evidence — the sentence that proves the change. Detective work, done together.

🎉 Now a fresh case, all yours…

⭐ Your turn, Kaitlyn
“Bees do much more than make honey. As bees visit flowers to drink nectar, pollen sticks to their bodies and travels with them. This helps plants make seeds, so new plants can grow. Many of the fruits and vegetables people eat exist because bees carry pollen from flower to flower.”

The main idea is: Bees help plants — and our food — grow. Which sentence from the passage is the best EVIDENCE for it?

🦉 So remember: main idea = the whole text in one line; evidence = the exact sentence that proves it. Always point at the sentence.

5

Argument writing: claim, evidence, reasoning

⭐
NY Next Generation · ELA Writing — Write arguments with reasons & evidence
🦉

Writing time, Kaitlyn! An argument isn't a fight — it's building a case so a reader says “okay, I'm convinced.” It has three parts, and I'll build one with you, brick by brick.

📖 Words to know: a claim is what you want the reader to believe. Evidence is a fact, number or example that backs it up. Reasoning is the sentence that explains WHY the evidence proves the claim. An opinion (“it's the best!”) is a feeling — it is NOT evidence.

👀 Watch me — I'll build one first

Step 1 — CLAIM: “Our school day should start later.” Short, clear, arguable. That's my case.

Step 2 — EVIDENCE: “Doctors say most teenagers need about 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night, and teenage brains naturally fall asleep late.” A fact — not a feeling.

Step 3 — REASONING: “If school starts before tired brains have slept enough, students learn less in first period — so a later start matches how teenage brains actually work.” See how it connects the fact back to the claim?

Step 4. Claim says it. Evidence backs it. Reasoning ties the knot. C–E–R.

✅ Three bricks: claim, evidence, reasoning — in that order.

🦉 Quick check, Kaitlyn

How is that sitting? No wrong answer here — I just want to know how to help.

A different way — a courtroom: The claim is the verdict you want. Evidence is what the detective brings in — real things people can check. Reasoning is the lawyer's closing line: “and THAT is why the evidence proves it.” Feelings (“I just think so”) get thrown out of court.

🤝 Try with me — we build one together

Our topic: school gardens. Claim (I'll give you this one): “Our school should have a garden.”

Step 1: Which of these is real EVIDENCE for the claim?

✔️ You spotted evidence over opinion — 12 pounds is checkable. That's the writer's eye!

Step 2: Which sentence is the REASONING — the one that ties the evidence to the claim?

✔️ Claim + evidence + reasoning — a complete argument, built by you and me.

🎉 Now judge one on your own…

⭐ Your turn, Kaitlyn

Claim: “Students should get a longer recess.” Which sentence is EVIDENCE — not opinion?

🦉 So remember: claim says it, evidence (checkable facts — never feelings) backs it, reasoning ties the knot.

6

Photosynthesis: matter & energy in plants

⭐
NYSSLS · Science MS-LS1-6 — Matter & energy in organisms
🦉

Science, Kaitlyn! Plants look quiet, but inside every leaf a tiny factory is running: photosynthesis. It takes simple things in, and builds food. Let's walk the factory floor together.

📖 Words to know: photosynthesis means “building with light.” Carbon dioxide is a gas in the air (the one you breathe OUT). Glucose is a sugar — the plant's food, where the sunlight's energy gets stored.

☀️ Sunlight
+ 💧 Water
+ 🌬️ Carbon dioxide→🌿 The leaf factory
(photosynthesis)→🍬 Glucose (food)
+ 🌬️ Oxygen
released into the air
👀 Watch me — let's trace it through

Step 1 — INPUTS in: The plant takes in three things: sunlight, water (from roots), and carbon dioxide (from the air).

Step 2 — THE BUILD: In the leaf, those pieces get rearranged — taken apart and rebuilt into something new. The sunlight provides the energy for the building.

Step 3 — OUTPUTS out: The factory makes glucose (sugar — the plant's food, storing the energy) and oxygen, which floats out into the air — the oxygen we breathe!

Step 4. Nothing appears from nowhere: the sugar's matter came from the air and water, and its energy came from the sun.

✅ In: light + water + carbon dioxide. Out: sugar + oxygen.

🦉 Quick check, Kaitlyn

How is that sitting? No wrong answer here — I just want to know how to help.

A different way — a bakery: A leaf is a bakery. Flour and water (the matter) go in; the oven's heat (the energy — sunlight) bakes them into bread (glucose). The lovely smell drifting out is like the oxygen released. Ingredients in, energy to build, new product out.

🤝 Try with me — a plant problem

A plant sits in a dark closet. It gets watered, and air reaches it. Something is missing…

Step 1: Which INPUT is the closet plant missing?

✔️ No light, no energy for building. You traced the missing input!

Step 2: So what happens to that plant over time?

✔️ Exactly — inputs decide outputs. Science reasoning, together.

🎉 Your turn — one quick product question…

⭐ Your turn, Kaitlyn

A healthy plant in sunlight is busy photosynthesising. What does it RELEASE into the air?

🦉 So remember: sunlight + water + carbon dioxide → glucose + oxygen. Matter gets rearranged; energy from sunlight gets stored in the sugar.

7

Ecosystems: the Hudson River food web

⭐
NYSSLS · Science MS-LS2 — Ecosystems: interactions, energy & dynamics
🦉

More science, Kaitlyn — close to home this time! The Hudson River and Long Island Sound, right by Port Chester, are full of living things that depend on each other. Tug one thread of the web, and the whole web moves.

📖 Words to know: an ecosystem is a community of living things plus their home. A food web shows who eats whom — arrows point from the food to the eater (following the energy). Interdependent means they all lean on each other.

🌿 Phytoplankton
(tiny floating plants)→🦐 Zooplankton
(tiny animals)→🐟 Small fish
(silversides, killifish)→🐠 Striped bass
+ 🦅 osprey & heron
👀 Watch me — trace the web with me

Step 1. Sunlight grows phytoplankton — tiny floating plants. (Hello again, photosynthesis!)

Step 2. Tiny animals, zooplankton, eat the phytoplankton. Then small fish eat the zooplankton.

Step 3. Striped bass — and birds like osprey and herons — eat the small fish. Energy flows up the chain, meal by meal.

Step 4. So every creature holds threads for others: the bass needs the small fish; the small fish need the zooplankton; everything needs the phytoplankton.

✅ One web, many threads: remove one species, and its eaters AND its food both feel it.

🦉 Quick check, Kaitlyn

How is that sitting? No wrong answer here — I just want to know how to help.

A different way — a seesaw: Picture predators and their food on a seesaw, balanced. Remove lots of the food, and the predator side sinks — hungry predators decline. Remove the predators, and the food side pops UP — nothing is eating them. Every change tips the seesaw two ways.

🤝 Try with me — tug a thread together

A disease wipes out most of the small fish in the Sound one summer. Predict with me…

Step 1: What most likely happens to the striped bass?

✔️ Predators feel it when food vanishes. One direction of the seesaw — nailed.

Step 2: And what happens to the zooplankton, now that few fish are eating them?

✔️ Both directions! Food up, eaters down — that's real ecosystem prediction.

🎉 Now predict one solo…

⭐ Your turn, Kaitlyn

Suppose the ospreys disappeared from Long Island Sound. What would most likely happen to the small fish that ospreys eat?

🦉 So remember: in a food web, removing a species tips things twice — its food increases, and its eaters struggle. Everything is connected.

8

From the Articles to the Constitution

⭐
NY Social Studies Framework · Grade 7 — History of the United States
🦉

History, Kaitlyn! America's first plan for a government didn't work — and the fix became the Constitution, the plan still used today. This is a story of a problem and a repair. Let's walk it slowly.

📖 Words to know: a confederation is a loose team of independent states. The Constitution is the written plan for the U.S. government. Checks and balances means each branch of government can limit the others, so nobody gets too powerful.

👀 Watch me — the story in steps

Step 1 — Plan A: After independence, the states teamed up under the Articles of Confederation (1781). Each state stayed almost like its own country.

Step 2 — The weakness: The national government could not collect taxes and had no president and no national courts. It couldn't pay soldiers or settle fights between states.

Step 3 — The warning: When farmers in Massachusetts protested (Shays' Rebellion), the national government was too weak to help. Leaders realised Plan A was failing.

Step 4 — Plan B: In 1787, delegates met in Philadelphia and wrote the Constitution: a stronger national government with three branches — Congress makes laws, the President carries them out, courts judge them — each checking the others. The Bill of Rights was added in 1791 to protect people's freedoms.

✅ Story shape: weak plan → real problems → stronger plan with safety checks.

🦉 Quick check, Kaitlyn

How is that sitting? No wrong answer here — I just want to know how to help.

A different way — a team with no captain: Imagine a soccer team where nobody can collect money for uniforms, there's no captain and no referee, and every player makes their own rules. Chaos — right? That's the Articles. The Constitution gave the team a captain (President), a rulebook committee (Congress) and referees (courts) — but each one can be overruled by the others, so nobody becomes a boss of everything.

🤝 Try with me — match the problem to the fix

Step 1: Problem — “Congress couldn't collect taxes, so the country couldn't pay its soldiers.” Which fix does the Constitution give?

✔️ Problem matched to its fix. That's how historians read this story!

Step 2: Problem — “One person with all the power could become a tyrant.” What's the Constitution's safety device?

✔️ Power split three ways, each branch checking the others. You've got the whole story now.

🎉 Last question of the set — it's yours…

⭐ Your turn, Kaitlyn

Which problem did the Constitution fix?

🦉 So remember: the Articles made the national government too weak; the Constitution made it stronger — and split it into three branches that check each other.

🌿 The Montessori way — Real Occupations & Self-Construction

Montessori's plan for adolescents is not more worksheets — it's real work in a real community, with real outcomes. The Creators path is built exactly on it:

  • Occupations, not subjects: Volcano Lab, the film studio and the garden are occupations — science, maths, writing and research are learned because the work genuinely needs them.
  • Make something the world can use: the Toy Lab is a small Montessori micro-economy — design a thing, print it, present it, gift it or share it. Work with a purpose beyond a grade.
  • Socratic discussion: the Creator discussion prompts follow Montessori seminar style: read, question, defend an idea with evidence, listen properly to the other side.
  • The adult steps back: at this age Hoot is a mentor, not a teacher — the young person plans the week, keeps the journal and judges the finished work. That independence is the curriculum.

    AGES 14–18High School Learning Path

    Eight core lessons behind this semester's courses. Each teaches the actual concept — worked through, not just named — then a quick check proves it landed. The planner, flashcards and practice test above turn these into daily reps.

    Connecticut standards: Connecticut Core Standards, NGSS science and CT Social Studies Frameworks for Grades 9–12, organised as transcript-ready courses — Biology, Algebra II, U.S. History and Spanish II this semester — with credits tracked as each course is completed.

    📖 How this path works: learn the concept, then check it. Mentor Hoot teaches each concept step by step — tap Next step ▶ to reveal the worked reasoning one move at a time, with real terminology and plain-meaning glosses where a word is doing heavy lifting. Tap the diagrams, flows and verdict cards in every lesson to interrogate them yourself. Each lesson closes with a So remember recap, and ▶ Show me again, Hoot! replays the teaching — then one question confirms it stuck.

    ⭐ 0 of 8 lessons done

    1

    Biology: where energy comes from

    ⭐

    Every cell runs on ATP — energy currency. The mitochondria mint it: they take glucose from food plus oxygen from breathing and convert them into ATP. Muscles, brain, everything spends it. That's why you breathe faster when you run: your cells are demanding more ATP, so the mitochondria need more oxygen. (Yes — this is flashcard #1 above, now explained.)

    Check it! Which organelle produces most of a cell's ATP?

    2

    Algebra II: keep the balance

    ⭐

    Solving an equation means getting x alone — and an equation is a balance: whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other. Worked example:

    x + 5 = 12  →  subtract 5 from BOTH sides  →  x = 7

    Check: 7 + 5 = 12 ✓. Every equation in set 5.3 is this same move — undo what's been done to x, one step at a time.

    Check it! x + 7 = 15. What is x?

    3

    History: a thesis is a claim

    ⭐

    Friday's essay stands or falls on its thesis — and a thesis is a claim you must prove, not a topic. Weak: “This essay is about the transcontinental railroad.” That announces a subject; it argues nothing. Strong: “The transcontinental railroad reshaped American migration by cutting a six-month journey to one week.” Specific, arguable, and provable with evidence — every paragraph can now do a job.

    Check it! Which of these is a real thesis?

    4

    Study science: test, don't re-read

    ⭐

    Memory research is blunt: retrieval practice beats re-reading. Forcing your brain to pull an answer out — flashcards, self-quizzing — strengthens the memory far more than looking at the page again, and spreading short sessions across days (spacing) beats one long cram. That's why the planner above schedules 10-minute flashcard reviews instead of one Sunday marathon.

    Check it! The night before a test, which method works best?

    5

    Biology: DNA to protein

    ⭐

    Module 7's second half: DNA is the instruction set. Its code stays protected inside the nucleus, but proteins are built OUTSIDE it — a messenger copy (mRNA) carries one gene's instructions to a ribosome, which reads the code and assembles the matching protein, amino acid by amino acid. DNA → message → protein: that single flow runs everything from muscle fibre to insulin.

    Check it! Where in the cell are proteins actually assembled?

    6

    Algebra II: two-step equations

    ⭐

    Two-step equations just need the balance move twice — undo in reverse order, last thing on, first thing off. Worked example:

    2x + 3 = 11  →  subtract 3: 2x = 8  →  divide by 2: x = 4

    Check: 2 × 4 + 3 = 11 ✓. Undo the addition first, then the multiplication — the whole second half of problem set 5.3 follows exactly this order.

    Check it! 3x + 4 = 19. What is x?

    7

    History: primary vs secondary sources

    ⭐

    Historians grade evidence by distance. A primary source was created AT the time, by someone who was there — a letter, a diary, a photograph, a ticket stub. A secondary source was made later, ABOUT the time — a textbook, a documentary, a museum label. Friday's essay gets stronger the moment a primary source walks into it: real voices beat summaries of voices.

    Check it! Which of these is a PRIMARY source for a railroad-era essay?

    8

    Spanish II: -ar verb endings

    ⭐

    Spanish II, Module 3's engine: regular -ar verbs change their ending to match WHO is acting. Take hablar (to speak): drop the -ar, then add — yo hablo, tú hablas, él/ella habla. Learn that one pattern and it unlocks hundreds of verbs: estudiar → estudio, bailar → bailo, trabajar → trabajo.

    Check it! Complete the sentence: «Yo ___ español.»

    💡 Fresh Ideas — new in Hoot's World

    Nine rituals that stretch the curriculum off the screen and into your real week — the last three are made just for ages 2–4. Each one takes minutes to set up, pairs with something already in the app, and works with whatever you have at home.

    🌅

    The Morning Basket

    A tray or basket set out the night before holding exactly three things: a book, one hands-on work, and one small surprise. Your child starts the day without ever asking "what do we do?" — the basket answers, and choice inside it is pure Montessori. — the basket holds today's first three steps.

    🏠 IndoorAt homePairs with…Today's Plan ↑
    ⭐

    The Family Star Jar

    A real jar on a real shelf. Every finished day-plan earns one marble, button or paper star dropped in together. When the jar is full, the family celebrates the way the child chooses — a picnic, a baking day, a library trip. Progress you can hold in two hands. — fill a jar in the game, too.

    🏠 IndoorAt homePairs with…Catch the Twinkle Stars
    📸

    Photo Quest Friday

    One photo mission every Friday: photograph something that changed this week — a leaf, a tower, a finished page, a taller sunflower. Print or save them in order and, month by month, they become a real growth album your child can flip through and narrate.

    🌳 OutdoorAt homePairs with…Real-World Adventures
    🌱

    The Bean Jar Lab

    Grow one bean in a jar of wet paper on the windowsill. Measure it with a ruler every Monday, draw it every Friday, and write one sentence about what changed. A single plant quietly teaches NGSS observation, measuring and patience in about three weeks.

    🏠 IndoorAt homePairs with…
    🎲

    Spin-the-Choice Wednesday

    Mid-week, hand over one real choice: replay a favourite step, swap two steps around, or take the whole day's plan outdoors. A rhythm with choices inside it never goes stale — freedom within limits is exactly how a Montessori day stays alive. — the original choose-your-work.

    🏠 IndoorAt homePairs with…the Work Shelf ↓
    🎤

    Showcase Sunday

    Ten minutes every Sunday: your child shows the family one thing from the week — a story line read aloud, a quest finding, a printed Toy Lab buddy, a quiz they wrote. Work with a real audience stops feeling like exercises and starts feeling like theirs.

    🏠 IndoorAt homePairs with…the Living Storybook & Toy Lab
    🧺

    The Treasure Basket · Ages 2–4

    A low basket of safe, real things from around the house — a wooden spoon, a pine cone, a soft scarf, a big shell, a metal whisk. No instructions at all: babies and toddlers learn by holding, shaking, mouthing and banging, and one basket quietly holds their attention longer than almost any toy. Swap a few things every Sunday so it is always a little bit new.

    🏠 IndoorAt home · Ages 2–4Pairs with…the Work Shelf ↓
    🧽

    Washing-Up Water Play · Ages 2–4

    A washing-up bowl of warm water, a few plastic cups and lids, and a towel on the floor. Scooping, pouring, stirring and squeezing a sponge is a whole morning for a 2- or 3-year-old — and it is the exact hand strength and concentration that Pouring Practice and Spoon Transfer build on the shelf.

    🏠 IndoorAt home · Ages 2–4Pairs with…Pouring & Spoon Transfer ↓
    🥁

    Shake & Freeze · Ages 2–4

    A shaker each — a sealed tub with rice or pasta inside does it. Shake, dance and wiggle while the music plays, then FREEZE like a statue when it stops. Listening, moving and stopping on purpose is self-control practice disguised as the silliest game in the house.

    🏠 IndoorAt home · Ages 2–4Pairs with…Dance Party
